verdict: Avoid new chemical, dye and intermediate exposure in Bharuch until unit-level safety and working-capital data are verified; lend only to established, compliant units with strong parentage and tight covenants.
title: Bharuch Chemicals, Dyes & Intermediates: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A Bharuch dye or intermediate unit buys petrochemical feedstock, runs multi-step batch reactions in reactors, and sells to textile, agrochemical and pharma buyers.** Cash is made on conversion margin, not on the molecule: value sits in reactor throughput, solvent recovery and the ability to pass feedstock cost through. **The working-capital cycle is the real credit risk** — inventory of feedstock and in-process material plus receivables from formulators tie up cash, and rating reports flag elevated working-capital intensity that blocks capital in high-growth scenarios [9]. Capex is reactor, boiler and effluent-treatment heavy, and rating commentary expects it to be met largely from internal accrual [8]. **So when a proposal lands, check the feedstock-to-product pass-through clause and the receivable days by buyer; if pass-through is absent, ask for the last four quarters' gross margin by product.**

## What has changed now
**National chemical output is shrinking while bank credit to the sector races ahead.** IIP for NIC 20 is -0.5% YoY and -1.2% Apr-to-date, against bank credit growth of +20.7% YoY — a gap of +21.9 pp [D]. That gap means lenders are funding inventory and receivables, not new demand. **Brent at $113/bbl sits above the $75–100 band [D], so feedstock and freight costs are elevated and margin depends on pass-through.** Locally, a Bharuch chemical unit explosion killed 5 workers and injured 5 on 16-Oct-2026 [3] — safety and consent compliance are now live credit issues, not just EHS. **So when a proposal lands, check the factory licence, consent-to-operate validity and last safety audit; if any is expired or pending, ask for the renewal receipt before appraisal.**

## Where the growth is
**Peer results show the split clearly: volume-led specialty players are winning.** Aarti Industries reported Q2 FY27 PAT up 60% to Rs. 169 crore on 30% volume growth [5], with revenue up 75% to ₹3,668 crore [6] and record quarterly revenue and EBITDA [4][7]. **Pursue borrowers who are qualified suppliers into such specialty chains** — long-term supply agreements, export-qualified, with fuel-additive or agrochemical intermediate lines. **Avoid commodity dye and generic intermediate units selling into spot domestic markets**, where Chinese dumping and de-stocking hit revenue (rating commentary notes a 9% dip last fiscal on pricing pressure and de-stocking) [8]. Local project-tracker pages list new chemical and synthetic-organic projects in Gujarat [1][2], but they carry no borrower-level financials — treat them as a pipeline list only.

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the working-capital cycle, not the balance sheet.** Fund receivables and inventory with a cash-flow-tied limit, not a term loan for expansion until the unit shows two quarters of stable throughput. **Take every month: stock-and-receivable statement, feedstock purchase invoices, power and steam consumption, and consent-compliance status.** Covenant on pass-through: if gross margin falls below the trailing four-quarter average, the limit freezes. **For capex, insist on internal-accrual funding with minimal external debt, as rating commentary expects [8]; if the borrower proposes debt-funded expansion, ask for the project report and phasing.**

## Early-warning signs
**Watch the credit-to-output gap at borrower level.** If a unit's drawing power rises while power consumption and dispatches are flat, the limit is funding unsold stock — freeze and inspect. **Watch receivable days by buyer; if a single formulator crosses a third of receivables, ask for that buyer's payment record.** Watch consent and safety status: any notice after the Bharuch incident [3] means stop fresh disbursement. **Watch feedstock pass-through; if Brent stays above the band [D] and the borrower's margin compresses, the unit is absorbing cost it cannot recover.**
watch: Drawing power rises while dispatches flat for two months -> freeze limit and inspect godown
Single buyer crosses one-third of receivables -> seek that buyer's payment record and credit insurance
Notice or lapse after Bharuch incident [3] -> stop fresh disbursement until renewal
Monthly feedstock invoice vs product price
Margin below trailing four-quarter average -> invoke pass-through covenant and reprice
